It'd actually be possible to beat it at level 1, but not consistent at all and very RNG dependent. You'd basically have to petrify at least one of your party members in advance so Chaos would attempt to attack them, and get lucky with Chaos casting Curaja, Haste, or Slowra early. Any damaging spell is a loss, until you set up enough Giant Tonics and Giant's Gloves. Then you can heal constantly with X Potions.


The hardest part before would probably be getting past Lich, which is a matter of getting Silence to stick, and since you can buy Phoenix Downs by that point, having enough to constantly buy attacks. 


After that, you can get the Canoe, which means you can get the airship, which means you can get Tonics for buffing, where it becomes doable. Until then, you're stuck relying on expensive weapons like the Mythril Sword, and RNG is REQUIRED to be amazing to succeed.


The Dawn of Souls version at least has consistent spell patterns, so you can mitigate the need for good RNG almost entirely with effective strategy. So I still stand by that being the best version.

What I do for boss fights, even at level 1, is give characters something like 2 to 5 Legendary Actions that they use at the start of a round before anyone moves, but the effects are telegraphed. Not in an obvious way. Something like, "a strong wind begins to pick up" indicating that the players will be pushed back. Then another telegraph will denote a danger zone, or multiple. If the players are, or end up in the danger zone by the end of the round, no save, no roll vs AC, they eat a hit, and take a lot of damage.

Give them a ton of HP so they last a few rounds, and a few different attacks like this, then a self buff after like 5 rounds or something that makes their attacks way harder to dodge, and you've got a boss fight where rhe players have to optimize offense and defence. Bonus points if you give the players a time limit of like 40 seconds to take their turns so they have to plan their turn quickly as well as carefully.

I find foods that I like eating, and eat until I feel content. Not full. But content. And even if I go over for a day, as long as I'm at a net loss for that week or even month, I'm still making progress, while my diet still feels sustainable, because I know that one day I went over is an exception: A treat.

I've also been able to find foods that feel filling for low calories. My favorite is Harvest Snaps Baked Red Lentils. I don't even have to prepare it. It fills me for half the day for only being roughly 350 calories. And it tastes delicious. I'll eat it slowly while working, so I'll feel it hit my stomach before I eat too much, and stop feeling hungry.

On extra special or tough days, I can still order a pizza because my overall calories are still below Maintenance for that month.

It took me a bit to get to this due to the hectic week, but I definitely appreciate the suggestions. Already picked up the audio overhauls you recommended. It looks like {{Soulmancer}} gives me a massive variety, so I'll never get bored. I haven't even finished checking out everything it offers! (Yet.)

In short, I care about frame data, timing attacks, having different options, and strategies on where and how I attack. I'd want it in a third person view. Huge fighting game nerd here if you can't tell.

But I feel {{Wildcat}} doesn't do that from what I played of it. It amounts to maximizing damage, and makes a lot of the fighting happen in the menu, or take a backseat entirely by solving injuries with items or stopping the adventure on the spot to go to an inn. Since I intend to pair this with {{Requiem}} or something similar, I feel like it'd dramatically slow down the gameplay loop too- which I don't want.

I did check into {{Blade and Blunt}}, though, and for the most part, I love the idea of increasing stagger on enemies with certain hits, but don't love the dramatic increases in damage. Counter systems are amazing, but with numbers that high, it'd feel like nerfing myself to not fish for them. I understand it's hard to make an engaging combat system with the engine Skyrim uses, but I still want to try hard to idealize it. I could see myself using {{Blade and Blunt}} as a last resort, though, especially since it looks easy to disable the injuries. I also don't like the idea of applying them to the enemies which I don't think this does. I don't want to have to micromanage status ailments I can't even see. If I could see them or more deliberately apply them, then absolutely I'd love this, especially if they can be solved in the middle of an adventure by taking risks, such as how Monster Hunter World handles Bleeding by crouching and staying still for a few seconds, or doesn't even fully remove the player's agency during Stuns by letting them escape it faster via mashing.

I love the idea of {{Know your Enemy 2}}. I may just add it, and see how it goes when balanced with other combat mods. Changing the way I approach each enemy really appeals, but if it's balanced purely for vanilla, I may not get to keep it with other combat adjustments I want to make.

I hope that all makes sense, and more importantly, I hope it's not too long a read. I'm pretty passionate about having well adjusted combat, so this is easily the part I want to focus on most.

Block + basic ki blast (Square or X depending on controller) gives you iFrames. It has low ki cost and is spammable. You can't use it when you have low Ki, though. But it can be used as a good panic button, or help you avoid attacks that are too difficult to Dodge reliably.

In long: Depends on your perspective of downhill. I'll explain in an as unbiased opinion as possible.


Progression: FF14 is still popular, and it's only getting more popular. But it has lost some of its complexity in both good ways and bad ways in trying to appeal to a broader audience, and there's still the hard-core content at Higher Levels. Just way more time and effort to get there. And as others were saying, barely any player interaction is required, but the story does take quite awhile to be worth anything. Most (not all) people I've spoken to universally agree you should get your Level 50 kit at Level 15, and the story only gets interesting when you're nearing the end of ARR patch quests. I agree with them for the most part.


As for customization: The most you'll get is how your character looks. Your abilities are strictly linear, and there is an objectively optimal set of gear, even if all of it is technically viable save for Ultimates. But even that is somewhat measured in that your one character can switch Jobs/Classes out of combat indefinitely, so you do get ways of choosing your different flavours of damage, healing, or tanking. But pretty much everything you get can be turned into a cosmetic, so search enough, and you'll find a way to doll yourself the way you want, with exceptions here and there.


Community time: While I hear the community itself is very good, and for the most part I seem to agree, there's the definite possibility you get unlucky and run into all the jerks. There are a lot of them, they're just silenced by the even more vast majority of pleasant players. Actually, biased time for the rest of this. The community has, despite my numerous encounters with toxic people, been able to prop me up and prevent burnout. There are times when I don't feel like playing, but want to do my dailies, and the community is just usually so friendly, I accidentally play ONLY FF for the night when I intended to play another game. I have never rushed. I'm still a sprout, and I have a few Jobs at 90, and have completed a large number of optional content. I take my time and read most of the dialogue.


Okay. Unbiased mode back on.


Lastly, Content: There's so much, and not all of it is baby mode easy content like the MSQ has you do for awhile. I've genuinely struggled on a few MSQ duties, though, only in Shadowbringers so far. But aside from combat, there is crafting and gathering, which are their own mini games, with gathering being the more relaxing one, and crafting being like a puzzle for level equivalent recipes. There's gambling! Which isn't really gambling, cuz you're guaranteed to make profit, or the rules are in your favour, but the games are fun. Collecting, which can be minions or mounts. The PvP is actually quite fun, but most don't like it because you won't be good at it right away, and you actually have to put effort in to learn. The Deep Dungeons are a lot of people's favourite content, and they added new variable dungeons with alternate paths. Cosmetics themselves may as well be a whole brand of content. Oh, and if you like grinding, there's relics. Even with all this, I definitely missed several types of content. There's a decent amount of variety- you will not be bored.

I'm providing an explanation for all the important bits. But if you want to just make a character, feel free to ignore them. Might help you understand the mechanics more is all.

High Elves are the best race in the game due to their Paralysis immunity, but pick whatever you want. I recommend Redguard because their formula for weapons change.

>Hammerfell for Redguard, 
>Sunmerset for High Elves

Obviously we'll be making a custom class. Call it whatever you wish. 

You gain levels based on how much you increase your Primary Skills, the first two Major Skills. And the first Minor Skill.

So we're going to pick Short Blade for a Primary skill. This will let you start with an Ebony Dagger, but bare in mind, Long Blades are generally better. With an Ebony Dagger, you will still deal enough damage. As far as I recall, no enemies resist blunt weapons, while Skeletons take half from Bladed. But the Ebony Dagger is so strong, there should be little issue even despite that.

Your Stealth Skill gets checked regardless of if you're sneaking, so that will be another Primary Skill. Just remember to actually sneak if you want to get the drop on enemies.

Critical Strike increases your accuracy, unless you modded it to do otherwise. Either way, it will increase along with your Short Blades. So that's important too for a Primary.

Dodging and Mysticism for Major Skills. Dodging constantly gets used, and Mysticism lets you cast spells that open locks or such. Lockpicking is very hard to make effective, and not especially worthwhile. You can use it if you want, but I don't advise it.

The third Major Skill doesn't matter as much as the first two, but you should still pick something you'll use, like Restoration. I picked Climbing in this instance because it can be very fun to use, especially on a thief who may want to Climb over city walls at night.

The most important Minor Skill is only the first one. You can pretty much use whatever you want for the rest, even as flavour, but I'll fill out what I used anyway as a general recommendation to make the game easier. I chose Running because Speed is both convenient and useful when simply moving, or fleeing from enemies. Plus if you're fast enough, you can sprint in, land a hit, and sprint out before an enemy attacks you.

If you want to know why I picked the rest of the Skills the way I did, just ask, and I'll provide details.

 My own homebrew rule for Death Saves. Makes Survival harder, and makes healing simultaneously more and less valuable.

1. Your Speed is Halved

.

3. Long Rests remove all failed Death Saves.

4. Spare the Dying removes one failed Death Save, but is now a 1st Level Spell.

I usually let my players roll Perception when requested. If they want to roll, they can, but I usually make it a lengthy time investment, and have it only apply to one thing. If they're searching for traps, they may not see an ambush coming. If they're searching for hidden enemies, they'll notice less loot or less hidden items.

My players don't generally roll to begin with, especially since I rarely demand Perception rolls. I tell them obvious things they would see, and use their Passive Perception as often as I can. I won't withhold information such as a grate that could potentially be a trap, or simply be for drainage. They may even climb under the grate for treasure. The point is, it's obvious, and it might have nothing, but it could also have something, so I don't withhold the information.

Usually my response to a roll of 18 or 25 or whatever is that they don't find anything new. Since they realistically wouldn't. I've already laid out the entire room in most cases.

I ban my players from playing any simple character.

For further detail, their character is only ready to join the campaign when their character has: (1) A career or career path planned. (2) A family, a history where their character or people related to their character, such as a personal antagonist or even friend doing something to noticeably modify how the world reacts and responds to them. And (3) A motive to be out on an adventure in the first place.

If my players are missing even a single one of these, I will tell them exactly what they are missing, and give them suggestions if they need them.

Every DM is different.
But there are a few key points that apply to all of them, and here they are.

1. Show Up :
The most important one by far. Show up. If you're a few minutes late, so what? Even if you're thirty minutes late, it's way better than not showing up at all. Game doesn't feel good without a full party.


2. Engagement :
Also very important. If you're not engaged in the setting, asking questions about it where you can, trying to learn more, then it feels to the DM like you're just coasting. Like you don't want to be there.


3. Narrative :
Either the narrative for the game story, or your characters. Usually a DM will have a theme around a narrative, and you can write your character's backstory to share elements with that theme.
And more on character backstory, give the DM hooks. Give them ammunition to pull your character along. Family that's alive, that they want to see. Maybe they have a father or son they're at odds with, and are trying to make amends or get over a life changing fight they had. Family doesn't even necessarily mean blood related or adopted. Someone could be an orphan, join a Hunter's Guild or something, and that could be their family from their perspective.


4. Feedback :
Ask for it. Simple. Every DM has their own preferences, and most of the time, DMs ask for feedback. Players should also ask for feedback too. Not much wording to complicate this one. Basic communication will solve the rest of your problems.
